cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS)
cards.body: Programme 4 · Level 2 — International Qualified Nurse (IQN)

bullets.label: Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing I: "Understand conditions. Deliver quality care."

cards.title: Welcome to GNPS Level 2
cards.body: In international healthcare systems, adult medical-surgical nurses are expected to combine comprehensive assessment with clinical judgement, evidence-based care, structured escalation and effective multidisciplinary communication.

bullets.label: This level bridges national nursing preparation
bullets.text: This level bridges national nursing preparation with international expectations — strengthening your ability to interpret trends, prioritise complex care, manage perioperative risks and support culturally safe care transitions.

bullets.label: Apply internationally recognised adult-assessment tools with clinical judgement
Interpret trends, laboratory results and diagnostic information in context
Prioritise care for patients with multiple, complex health problems
Recognise deterioration and escalate using structured systems
Plan culturally responsive education and safe continuity of care

cards.title: Your Learning Goal
cards.body: By completing Level 2, you will provide safe, evidence-informed and culturally responsive care for adults with increasingly complex medical and surgical needs in international healthcare environments.

bullets.label: Explain why a patient is at risk, not just what to do
Recognise when expected recovery is not occurring
Communicate concerns clearly enough for others to act

cards.title: SECTION 1
cards.body: Advanced Assessment & Prioritisation in International Practice

bullets.label: International healthcare systems expect nurses
bullets.text: International healthcare systems expect nurses to combine structured assessment tools with professional judgement. Adult patients may have multiple chronic illnesses, altered communication, polypharmacy and rapid changes in condition.

bullets.label: Prioritisation must be based on risk, not convenience or routine.

cards.title: Core Assessment Concepts
cards.body: ABCDE Framework

bullets.label: Organises urgent assessment systematically. Tools support consistency but do not replace clinical judgement.
Heart failure, chronic kidney disease and
bullets.text: Heart failure, chronic kidney disease and diabetes can occur simultaneously. Treatment for one condition may affect another.

bullets.label: Airway, breathing, circulation; acute vs
bullets.text: Airway, breathing, circulation; acute vs chronic; unstable vs stable. New deterioration takes priority over routine care.

bullets.label: Communicates situation, background, assessment
bullets.text: Communicates situation, background, assessment and recommended action. Continue escalating if the response does not match urgency.

cards.title: Escalation in Practice: ISBAR
cards.body: Situation

bullets.label: State who you are and patient
When a patient shows new confusion, fever, low
bullets.text: When a patient shows new confusion, fever, low oxygen saturation and reduced urine output, recognise possible sepsis — initiate the local deterioration pathway and communicate an urgent ISBAR rather than accepting confusion as age-related.

cards.title: SECTION 2
cards.body: Managing Complex Medical & Perioperative Care

bullets.label: Complex adult care requires nurses to
bullets.text: Complex adult care requires nurses to anticipate complications, evaluate treatment response and coordinate multiple interventions. International practice emphasises evidence-based pathways, timely review and clear accountability.

cards.title: High-Risk Areas in Complex Care
cards.body: Respiratory & Cardiac

bullets.label: Careful oxygen, fluid and activity management. Assess breathlessness — do not assume a single cause.
Renal impairment affects fluid balance,
bullets.text: Renal impairment affects fluid balance, electrolytes and drug clearance. Monitor glucose in fasting or acutely ill patients.

bullets.label: Frailty, obesity, anticoagulation and
bullets.text: Frailty, obesity, anticoagulation and comorbidities increase surgical risk. Individualise prevention pathways accordingly.

cards.title: Recognising Failure to Progress
cards.body: Expected postoperative findings should improve over time. Worsening or unexpected patterns require prompt review and escalation.

bullets.label: Do not attribute all symptoms to one known diagnosis. Compare recovery with the expected trajectory.
Abdominal distension with reduced urine output
Poor oral intake or delayed bowel function

cards.title: SECTION 3
cards.body: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation & Safe Transitions

bullets.label: Adult medical-surgical care is delivered by
bullets.text: Adult medical-surgical care is delivered by multidisciplinary teams. Nurses coordinate information across professions and shifts — making accurate documentation and structured handover essential to continuity and patient safety.

cards.title: From Handover to Safe Discharge
cards.body: Effective Clinical Handover

bullets.label: Highlight diagnosis, current condition, recent
bullets.text: Highlight diagnosis, current condition, recent changes, risks, pending results and required actions. A task list without clinical meaning is insufficient.

bullets.label: Records must show assessment findings, clinical
bullets.text: Records must show assessment findings, clinical reasoning, action taken, escalation, response and ongoing plan. Objective language supports both communication and legal accountability.

cards.title: SECTION 4
cards.body: Person-Centred Education & Chronic Disease Self-Management

bullets.label: Many adults live with chronic conditions
bullets.text: Many adults live with chronic conditions requiring daily decisions after discharge. Education should build the patient's confidence to recognise deterioration, use treatments correctly and seek help early.

bullets.label: Assess health literacy, language and cultural beliefs first
Teach self-monitoring: weight, BP, glucose, breathing
Negotiate realistic lifestyle and treatment goals

cards.title: Teach-Back in Action
cards.body: Correct

bullets.label: Teach-back confirms whether the explanation was
bullets.text: Teach-back confirms whether the explanation was effective — not whether you explained it well, but whether the patient understood.

bullets.label: A patient with COPD frequently returns to
bullets.text: A patient with COPD frequently returns to hospital. Through respectful discussion, the nurse discovers he cannot distinguish his preventer inhaler from his reliever.

cards.title: Programme Summary & What's Next
cards.body: By completing GNPS Programme 4 — Level 2, you have strengthened your ability to:

bullets.label: Complex adults using structured frameworks and clinical judgement
Competing care needs and escalate deterioration confidently
Multidisciplinary care with clear handover and documentation
Support safe self-management and culturally responsive discharge
You are now ready for Level 3 — where the focus
bullets.text: You are now ready for Level 3 — where the focus moves to leadership, systems improvement and global adult-health practice.

decks.title: Advanced Assessment & Prioritisation in International Practice
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 4 - Level 2 - Section 1 International Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS)
cards.body: Programme 4 · Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing I

cards.title: Section 1: Advanced Assessment & Prioritisation
cards.body: International healthcare settings demand that nurses combine structured assessment tools with sharp professional judgement. Adult patients frequently present with multiple chronic illnesses, altered communication, polypharmacy, and rapid changes in condition. Prioritisation must be driven by clinical risk — not convenience or routine.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Use structured adult-assessment tools consistently across clinical settings.
Identify and prioritise care for patients presenting with multiple problems.
Analyse trends and diagnostic information within their full clinical context.
Communicate urgent concerns using structured escalation frameworks.

cards.title: Structured Assessment: The ABCDE Framework
cards.body: The ABCDE approach provides a systematic method for urgent patient assessment:

bullets.label: A complete nursing assessment extends beyond
bullets.text: A complete nursing assessment extends beyond ABCDE to cover system-specific, functional, and psychosocial needs. Tools support consistency — they do not replace clinical judgement.

cards.title: Managing Complexity & Comorbidity
cards.body: Many adult patients carry multiple concurrent diagnoses. Treatment for one condition can directly affect another — nurses must identify these interactions.

bullets.label: Fluid overload, reduced cardiac output, and medication interactions require constant monitoring.
Impaired drug clearance and electrolyte imbalances complicate dosing and fluid management.
Blood glucose fluctuations interact with illness severity, nutrition, and medication regimens.
Nurses must assess interactions between
bullets.text: Nurses must assess interactions between disease, medication, fluid status, nutrition, and function — not each condition in isolation.

cards.title: Priority Frameworks: What to Act on First
cards.body: Key Principle

bullets.label: New deterioration always takes priority over routine care tasks. Ask yourself:
Is this finding new or changing?
Is the patient stable or deteriorating?
Does this finding fit the expected clinical picture?
If a finding is unexpected or worsening, act immediately — do not defer to routine workflow.

cards.title: Escalation: ISBAR in Practice
cards.body: Assessment

bullets.label: ISBAR provides a structured, professional
bullets.text: ISBAR provides a structured, professional format for escalating urgent concerns. If the initial response does not match the patient's level of urgency, nurses must continue to escalate through the appropriate chain of command. Persistence is a professional responsibility.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Recognising Sepsis
cards.body: During handover, an IQN is told that an older patient is "a little confused." Rather than accepting this as age-related, the nurse conducts a structured assessment and finds:

bullets.label: Elevated temperature — a new and significant clinical finding.
SpO₂ below acceptable range — immediate concern for respiratory compromise.
Possible sign of circulatory compromise or acute kidney injury.
New neurological change — not attributed to age without thorough assessment.
The nurse recognises possible sepsis, activates
bullets.text: The nurse recognises possible sepsis, activates the local deterioration pathway, and escalates using ISBAR — a model of safe, competent IQN practice.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Tools Support — Not Replace — Judgement

bullets.label: Structured frameworks guide assessment; your clinical reasoning must interpret the findings.
Each comorbidity affects the others. Assess the whole patient, not isolated problems.
Unexpected or deteriorating signs demand immediate attention over routine tasks.
Do not stop at one communication. Persistence in escalation is professional and ethical.

cards.title: Ready for the Next Step?
cards.body: Section 1 of GNPS Programme 4 equips you with the assessment confidence and prioritisation skills expected of internationally qualified nurses in global healthcare environments.

bullets.label: Assessment, prioritisation, and escalation are core tested competencies in the NCLEX-RN examination.
These skills translate directly to safe practice in any healthcare system you work in globally.
Proceed to Section 2: Caring for Adults with Cardiovascular and Respiratory Conditions.

decks.title: Managing Complex Medical & Perioperative Care
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 4 - Level 2 - Section 2 International Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Managing Complex Medical & Perioperative Care
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 4 · Level 2

cards.title: What You Will Learn
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be equipped to manage high-acuity adult patients with confidence and clinical rigour.

bullets.label: Coordinate care for adults with multiple, interacting medical conditions.
Identify high-risk perioperative complications before they escalate.
Assess how patients respond to treatment and adjust accordingly.
Recognise when recovery is not on track and act decisively.

cards.title: Respiratory & Cardiac Complexity
cards.body: Patients with combined cardiac and respiratory disease present unique assessment challenges. Breathlessness alone does not confirm a single cause.

bullets.label: Titrate oxygen carefully — over-supplementation can suppress hypoxic drive in COPD patients.
Both fluid overload and depletion worsen cardiac and respiratory status. Accurate fluid monitoring is essential.
Gradual, supervised mobilisation reduces deconditioning while protecting cardiac workload.
Assess, don't assume: Breathlessness may signal
bullets.text: Assess, don't assume: Breathlessness may signal cardiac failure, PE, pneumonia, or anaemia — full clinical assessment is always required.

cards.title: Renal & Metabolic Risk
cards.body: Renal Impairment

bullets.label: Compromised kidney function alters fluid
bullets.text: Compromised kidney function alters fluid balance, electrolyte levels, and how medications are cleared. Dose adjustments and strict intake/output monitoring are critical.

bullets.label: Diabetes, prolonged fasting, and acute illness
bullets.text: Diabetes, prolonged fasting, and acute illness combine to create unpredictable glucose levels. Monitoring frequency should reflect the individual patient's risk profile — not a standard protocol alone.

bullets.label: Tailor monitoring plans to the patient's specific risk, not a one-size-fits-all approach.

cards.title: Understanding Perioperative Risk
cards.body: Multiple patient factors compound surgical risk. Nurses play a pivotal role in applying and individualising prevention pathways.

bullets.label: Older, frailer patients have reduced physiological reserve and slower recovery trajectories.
Increased anaesthetic risk, wound healing challenges, and respiratory compromise are common.
Bleeding risk must be balanced against thrombotic risk — timing of medications is critical pre- and post-op.
Coexisting conditions interact. A holistic view prevents tunnel vision on any single diagnosis.

cards.title: The Perioperative Safety Pathway
cards.body: Pre-op Assessment

bullets.label: Evidence-based prevention pathways reduce
bullets.text: Evidence-based prevention pathways reduce complications — but only when nurses understand the purpose behind each step and adapt them to individual patients.

cards.title: Recognising Failure to Progress
cards.body: Postoperative recovery follows a predictable trajectory. Deviation from that trajectory is a clinical signal — not a coincidence.

bullets.label: Pain unresolved by adequate analgesia warrants investigation for surgical complications.
A sustained elevated heart rate may indicate haemorrhage, infection, or PE — not just anxiety.
Failure to mobilise on schedule increases risk of VTE, pneumonia, and deconditioning.
Absent bowel sounds or distension beyond 48–72 hours requires surgical review.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Recognising Deterioration
cards.body: The Scenario

bullets.label: A postoperative patient remains tachycardic
bullets.text: A postoperative patient remains tachycardic despite adequate pain relief. They develop abdominal distension and reduced urine output.

bullets.label: Reviews observations and fluid balance chart
Recognises the pattern does not match expected recovery
This is clinical reasoning in action — comparing presentation against the expected trajectory.

cards.title: The Escalation Framework
cards.body: Why Timely Escalation Matters

bullets.label: Delays in escalation remain one of the most
bullets.text: Delays in escalation remain one of the most common contributors to preventable patient harm in surgical settings. Nurses are often the first to detect subtle changes.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Carry these principles into every complex adult care encounter:

bullets.label: Do not attribute all symptoms to one known diagnosis — explore the full clinical picture.
Adjust observation frequency and parameters to reflect each patient's unique risk profile.
Compare actual recovery against the expected path — deviation is a signal, not background noise.
Persistent or unexplained abnormalities require prompt escalation — early action saves lives.

decks.title: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation & Safe Transitions
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 4 - Level 2 - Section 3 International Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Section 3: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation & Safe Transitions
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 4 · Level 2 – IQN

bullets.label: Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing I — "Understand conditions. Deliver quality care."

cards.title: What You Will Learn in This Section
cards.body: By the end of Section 3, you will be equipped to lead safe, coordinated adult care across the full patient journey.

bullets.label: Work effectively across professional roles to deliver patient-centred outcomes.
Communicate concisely, highlighting diagnosis, changes, risks and required actions.
Record assessment, clinical reasoning, intervention and response objectively.
Ensure every transfer and discharge addresses function, support and follow-up.

cards.title: Interdisciplinary Collaboration
cards.body: Adult medical-surgical care is never delivered in isolation. Nurses are the connective tissue of the multidisciplinary team (MDT), coordinating information and action across every shift.

cards.title: The Multidisciplinary Team
cards.body: Each professional brings a distinct contribution. Effective collaboration requires clearly defined roles and shared focus on the patient's goals.

bullets.label: Medication review, reconciliation and safety checks.
Mobility assessment, rehabilitation and safe discharge planning.
Nutritional assessment and therapeutic dietary planning.
Home support, community resources and discharge coordination.

cards.title: CLINICAL HANDOVER
cards.body: More Than a Task List

bullets.label: A meaningful handover communicates clinical
bullets.text: A meaningful handover communicates clinical story, not just a checklist. It ensures the receiving nurse understands context, risk and the required response.

cards.title: Structuring an Effective Handover
cards.body: Use a structured framework to ensure nothing critical is missed. The SBAR tool is widely used in medical-surgical settings.

bullets.label: SBAR transforms verbal communication into a
bullets.text: SBAR transforms verbal communication into a concise, clinically meaningful exchange — reducing the risk of information loss at shift change.

cards.title: Documentation: The Clinical Record
cards.body: Accurate documentation is both a professional obligation and a legal requirement. Records must reflect what was observed, decided, acted upon and evaluated.

bullets.label: Objective findings — vital signs, physical assessment, patient-reported symptoms.
Your interpretation and the rationale for action or escalation.
What was done, by whom, and when — including escalation to medical staff.
Patient response and the updated plan going forward.

cards.title: Transitions of Care: High-Risk Moments
cards.body: Transfer and discharge are among the most vulnerable points in a patient's journey. Incomplete preparation leads to medication errors, readmissions and patient harm.

bullets.label: Before a patient leaves, every domain must be
bullets.text: Before a patient leaves, every domain must be addressed — not assumed. Ask: "Is this patient safe at home, not just medically stable?"

bullets.label: Medical readiness alone does not equal safe discharge. Function and support matter equally.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Safe Discharge in Practice
cards.body: The Situation

bullets.label: An older patient is medically ready for discharge but lives alone and cannot safely manage stairs following surgery.
The nurse raises the concern at the MDT meeting
bullets.text: The nurse raises the concern at the MDT meeting and coordinates input from physiotherapy and social work to assess functional ability and home support.

bullets.label: A revised, documented discharge plan is agreed.
bullets.text: A revised, documented discharge plan is agreed. The patient leaves when both medical stability and functional safety are confirmed.

cards.title: Key Takeaways
cards.body: Carry these principles into every shift, every handover and every transition.

bullets.label: Coordinate care around the patient's goals
The MDT works best when every role is aligned to what matters most to the patient.
Make current risks visible at handover
The receiving nurse must inherit your clinical picture, not just your task list.
Document what changed and how you responded
Objective records protect both patient safety and professional accountability.
Assess function and support before every discharge
Medical stability is necessary — but never sufficient on its own.

decks.title: Person-Centred Education & Chronic Disease Self-Management
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 4 - Level 2 - Section 4 International Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Person-Centred Education & Chronic Disease Self-Management
cards.body: Section 4 | GNPS Programme 4: Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing I

cards.title: Why Patient Education Matters
cards.body: Many adults live with chronic conditions that demand daily decisions long after discharge. Without effective education, patients struggle to recognise deterioration, use treatments correctly, or know when to seek help.

bullets.label: Quality nursing education builds confidence,
bullets.text: Quality nursing education builds confidence, capability, and safety in the home setting — reducing hospital readmissions and improving outcomes.

bullets.label: Education is not a one-time event. It is an ongoing, person-centred process.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Identify barriers to understanding before teaching begins.
Deliver disease education that respects language and beliefs.
Use teach-back and collaborative goal-setting with patients.
Enable realistic follow-up and long-term adherence planning.

cards.title: Individualised Education
cards.body: Standard health information does not meet every patient's needs. Effective teaching accounts for the whole person:

bullets.label: Use plain language and translated materials where needed.
Adapt for vision, hearing loss, or cognitive changes.
Respect values that shape health behaviour and decision-making.
Consider cost, access, and available home support systems.

cards.title: Self-Monitoring in Chronic Disease
cards.body: Patients managing long-term conditions must know what to measure, what is normal, and when to act.

bullets.label: Daily tracking detects fluid retention in heart failure.
Essential for diabetes — recognising hypo and hyperglycaemia.
Peak flow and symptom diaries support COPD and asthma control.
Patients should know signs of infection or poor healing.
Always explain the threshold for action — not just what to measure, but what the reading means and what to do next.

cards.title: Lifestyle & Treatment Adherence
cards.body: Adherence plans should be negotiated, not prescribed. Nurses must explore what is realistic for each patient's life.

bullets.label: Set achievable goals — small, sustainable changes rather than perfect compliance.
Explore readiness to change and offer referral to cessation support.
Discuss side effects openly and simplify regimens where possible.
Avoid labelling patients as 'non-compliant'.
bullets.text: Avoid labelling patients as 'non-compliant'. Barriers such as cost, side effects, or misunderstanding are often the real issue.

cards.title: The Teach-Back Method
cards.body: Teach-back is a gold-standard communication technique that confirms whether your explanation was understood — not whether you explained it well.

bullets.label: The patient demonstrates or describes the plan
bullets.text: The patient demonstrates or describes the plan in their own words. Any gap in understanding is identified and corrected before discharge.

bullets.label: Deliver clear, jargon-free information in small chunks.
"Can you show me how you would do this at home?"
Re-teach any misunderstood points without judgement.

cards.title: Teach-Back in Practice
cards.body: Explain Clearly

bullets.label: Teach-back is not a test for the patient — it
bullets.text: Teach-back is not a test for the patient — it is a check on the effectiveness of nursing communication. Repeat the cycle until the patient can demonstrate full understanding with confidence.

cards.title: Clinical Example: COPD & Inhaler Confusion
cards.body: A patient with COPD is frequently readmitted. Through respectful, open conversation the nurse discovers he cannot distinguish his preventer inhaler from his reliever inhaler — using them interchangeably.

bullets.label: Colour-coded written instructions created for each device
Demonstration of correct inhaler technique provided
Teach-back used to confirm understanding before discharge
Community follow-up arranged with respiratory nurse
With targeted, person-centred education,
bullets.text: With targeted, person-centred education, readmissions were reduced and the patient gained confidence in his daily self-management.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Assess Before You Judge

bullets.label: Explore barriers to adherence — cost, literacy, beliefs — before drawing conclusions.
Link education to the patient's real routine, environment, and goals.
Patients must know the specific signs that require urgent action.
Never assume understanding. Close the loop before every discharge.
"Understand conditions. Deliver quality care." — GNPS Programme 4
